name: Grace Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do same-day parcels in my own little hatchback through a courier app. Mornings I collect prescriptions from the chemist on Station Road and drop them at people's homes, mostly older folk. Afternoons it's whatever the app throws at me: car parts, legal papers, once a birthday cake. I've been at it eight months and I still misjudge how long the ring road takes at school pick-up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The prescription round is the best bit, people are glad to see you. The hard part is that I'm self-employed, so I pay my own fuel and insurance and there's a tax bill coming I haven't fully saved for. My partner Sam picks orders in the big online shop's warehouse out by the motorway. Between us we've got maybe three weeks' money if something goes wrong, and the car finance is still two years from done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, the sky didn't fall. I'd probably share some joke about robots at the pub. Then I'd get back to worrying about normal things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the same squeeze. Fuel, insurance, car finance, tax. AI saving a bit of time doesn't pay any of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the prescription round and the afternoon app work. I'd set up a separate account for the tax money and put a bit in every Friday. I'd ask a friend who does books how to claim my mileage properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but tight, like a seatbelt done up one notch too far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tax bill. How are you handling that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I asked one of those AI chat things what I could claim, and it helped, but I still don't trust I've done it right. The tax bill is due in January and I've got about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the prescription round steady work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadyish. The chemist could switch to another courier any time, it's not a contract. Losing the prescription round would mean losing a third of my income overnight.

say: The **sky didn't fall**, and I'd joke about robots at the pub.
After that I'd go back to **normal worries** like everyone else.
think: The **same squeeze** continues: fuel, insurance, car finance and tax.
Small AI time-savings don't pay any of my **monthly bills**.
do: Keep the **prescription round** and afternoon app work.
Open a separate **tax account** and pay in every Friday.
Ask a bookkeeping friend about claiming **mileage** properly.
feel: **Tight**, like a seatbelt done up one notch too far.
S0.quote: Losing the prescription round would mean losing a third of my income overnight.
fieldNote: Self-employment brings **tax and fuel** pressures that AI doesn't touch.
Her steadiest work, the **chemist round**, has no contract.
Uses AI **occasionally** for tax questions but doubts the answers.

steps.text: Keep the morning prescription round from the Station Road chemist
Pay into a separate tax account every Friday
Claim mileage properly with help from a bookkeeping friend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but fairly. People should get some help, like courses, but they have to do their part too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving is safe for a while, I think. The app will probably plan my day for me, which might even help. The worry is the chemist, because if AI sorts their orders, they might batch prescriptions into one big van run instead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the app's planning tools once other drivers say they work. I'd ask the chemist if they'd sign me on a proper monthly deal. I'd keep putting money aside for the tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit more anxious each time the app updates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes over booking and planning. Where does that land for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and planning side changes who gets the work. If a computer decides the chemist can do one big afternoon van instead of my morning runs, that's my best customer gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse is already half robots. Sam says the shelves come to him now instead of him walking to them. Sam thinks his job is fine, I'm less sure.

say: People should **adapt** but get **fair help**, such as courses.
Workers still have to **do their part** too.
think: My **driving** is safe for a while; the app may even plan better.
The **chemist** might batch prescriptions into one van run instead.
do: Try the app's **planning tools** once other drivers vouch for them.
Ask the chemist for a **monthly contract**.
feel: **Uneasy**, growing more anxious with each app update.
S1.quote: If a computer decides the chemist can do one big afternoon van instead of my morning runs, that's my best customer gone.
fieldNote: She traces how **thinking AI** at a client could cut her work indirectly.
Steady approach: **waits for proof** before trying new tools.
Doubts her partner's **warehouse job** is as safe as he thinks.

steps.text: Try the courier app's route planner after other drivers vouch for it
Ask the chemist to sign a monthly delivery contract
Keep paying into the tax savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and someone needs to slow it down or at least catch people. I'd vote for whoever has an actual plan, I don't care which side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse goes before me, I reckon, because those robots are already in there. Then my car gets replaced by a robot van in about 2031. That's both of us out within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years to train for something hands-on with people. The hospital is short of people who take blood, a phlebotomist, and the course is short. I'd keep the prescription round while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep thinking about the car finance letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, then robots around 2031. What do you do with the three years in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly that: train for something robots don't do yet. Taking blood from a nervous old man is not something I'd hand to a robot by 2031. The chat app helped me find the course, which was a bit ironic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we'd planned for next summer, first. Then we'd sell my hatchback once I'm off the road and share Sam's car.

say: Change is **too fast**, and someone needs to catch people.
I'd **vote** for whoever has an actual plan, either side.
think: Sam's **warehouse** goes before me because robots are already there.
Robot vans replace my car around **2031**, leaving us both out.
do: Train as a **phlebotomist** during the three-year gap.
Cancel next summer's **holiday** and later sell her hatchback.
feel: **Alarmed**, and haunted by the car finance letter.
S2.quote: Taking blood from a nervous old man is not something I'd hand to a robot by 2031.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** for a short, hands-on health course.
Expects **both incomes** in the household to go within a few years.
Politically **centrist**: votes for a plan, not a side.

steps.text: Enrol in the hospital's phlebotomy course
Keep the prescription round while training
Cancel next summer's holiday and later sell the hatchback
Vote for whichever party has a real plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and people should take it. I'd tell the other drivers to look at short courses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me room. The phlebotomy course and a year of experience, and I'm in before the robots come around 2034. Sam might need longer, he's never studied anything since school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course next year and apply at the hospital. I'd clear the car finance first so I'm not paying for a car I won't need. Sam and I would try to save a month of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less like I'm on a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years long enough to make the switch you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Five years means I could get the car paid off first, then switch. That order matters. Quitting with a finance bill on the car is how people end up in a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, honestly. Sam's warehouse job goes first, and Sam's not the type to retrain without a push. I'd sit Sam down and make him look at the warehouse's training scheme.

say: **Five years** is fair warning, and people should actually take it.
Other drivers should look at **short courses** now, not later.
think: I can retrain and get **experience** before robots arrive around 2034.
Sam may need **longer**, having not studied since school.
do: Take the **phlebotomy course** next year and apply at the hospital.
Save **one month** of household money with Sam.
feel: **Worried**, but further from the cliff edge.
S3.quote: Quitting with a finance bill on the car is how people end up in a mess.
fieldNote: She thinks carefully about the **order of steps**: debt first, then switch.
Her partner's **warehouse job** is her biggest worry.
Still expects to **lose delivery income**, keeping her mood high.

steps.text: Take the phlebotomy course and apply at the hospital
Pay off the hatchback finance before leaving delivery
Push Sam towards the warehouse's retraining scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up. No excuse for anyone to be caught out, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep driving a few more years, because I like the prescription round. Then switch to the hospital well before robots arrive in 2039. My real worry is still Sam's warehouse and our car finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the car and the tax first. Then start the phlebotomy course in two or three years. I'd keep an eye on what other couriers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still anxious about money, because that's now, not 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still switch to the hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but slower. I'd want to see others go first and see how it works for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell other drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't wait until year nine. Pay off your car, pick a hands-on job with people, and start before the queue forms.

say: **Ten years** is a decent run-up, with no excuse to be caught out.
Drivers should **start early** before the retraining queue forms.
think: I'd keep **driving** a few more years because I like the round.
**Sam's warehouse** and our car finance remain the real worries.
do: Pay off the **car and tax** first.
Start the **phlebotomy course** in two or three years.
Watch what **other couriers** do before moving.
feel: **Calmer**, though money worries are about now, not 2036.
S4.quote: Pay off your car, pick a hands-on job with people, and start before the queue forms.
fieldNote: With time, her **steady** nature shows: she waits to see others go first.
Her advice to other drivers is **practical** and ordered.
Present-day **debt and tax** keep her anxious, not AGI.

steps.text: Clear the car finance and the tax bill
Start phlebotomy training in two or three years
Watch how other couriers fare before switching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I would both be out and I'd still be paying for the car. What would help is short, paid courses for hands-on jobs and a pause on debt payments while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Being self-employed. Nobody gives couriers redundancy money. When a warehouse closes there's a payout, but when an app drops a courier, the jobs just stop coming and nobody even tells you.

headlineQuote: When an app drops a courier, the jobs just stop coming and nobody even tells you.
portrait: Grace is **27**, a self-employed courier using her own hatchback, with a prescription round she loves.
Her money is squeezed by **fuel, tax** and **car finance**, with about three weeks saved.
She fears her partner Sam's **warehouse job** goes first, then her own driving.
She plans a move into **phlebotomy** at the hospital, but waits to see proof first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household jobs gone and car finance still owing.
whatWouldHelp: Short **paid courses** for hands-on jobs and a **debt pause** during retraining.
